From the 1960s to the mid-1980s about 20,000 Indigenous children in Canada were taken from their families and communities and adopted, mostly by non-Indigenous families. It is known as the Sixties Scoop (Government of Canada settlement, 2017)

Under Islamic law, children are raised through kafala (guardianship) instead of adoption. The child keeps their own name and their birth family's name

Adoptees who learned of their adoption late reported more feelings of betrayal and confusion about who they were than those told as children (Baden et al. 2019, a survey of US adoptees)
A child adopted from abroad grows up in the parents' culture at home but is treated as a racial minority outside. Researchers call it the transracial adoption paradox (Lee 2003)
Showing you the photos from the airport, your parents told you how you were born in {0} and came to this home on a plane.
Your parents told you that another woman gave birth to you, and that they took you in and have raised you since.
Your parents sat you down and told you that another woman gave birth to you, and that they had waited for you and adopted you. You did not understand it all, but their hands were warm.

A DNA test taken for fun listed relative after relative you had never heard of. You asked your parents, and learned for the first time that you were adopted.
From something a relative let slip, you learned you were adopted. Your parents were silent for a long time, then told you everything.

Once the first joy passed, you heard less often from your birth mother. You are still not sure what you should be to each other.

Now and then you meet your birth mother for tea, and little by little you tell each other the years you missed.
Your birth mother sends a small present on each of your children's birthdays.
The day your class drew family pictures, you thought for a long time, for the first time, about how your face in the mirror differed from your parents'.
You were teased at school about your looks. Your parents had never been through that and did not know what to say.

At the doctor's you left the family medical history blank. There was nothing to write.
For the first time, you held someone related to you by blood.
Applying for a passport, you found out you were not a US citizen. Your parents had never finished the naturalisation.

The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 gave citizenship only to adoptees who were under 18 then. Tens of thousands adopted from abroad who were already adults were left without it (Adoptee Rights Campaign)
Citizenship application
With a lawyer's help you applied, and at last took the oath. You became a citizen of the country you had lived in all your life.
Following the records, you found that the name and date on your papers belonged to another child. The trail ended there.
In 2025 Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission confirmed that adoption agencies had recorded children who had parents as orphans and swapped children's identities
You visited the orphanage and the place you were found, but there was no record anywhere of who had left you.
The records were only a few lines, and the trail ended there. You decided to look again someday.

Through the agency you found the mother who gave birth to you, but she sent word that she could not meet you yet. A short letter came.
In Korea, birth parents must agree before an adoptee is told about them. In 2024 birth parents' information was disclosed in 13.3% of cases (Segye Ilbo 2025)
